records.reason: Measure the pyridyl ketone at 2/1 with the same loading as measured 49201b5817f204116f7f at 5/1, which gave 47.37/119.31 mL and a historical V2 error of -60.38 mL. The current 2/1 prediction, 16.04/38.39 mL, tests whether that large retention develops over this solvent-strength change.

The tertiary amino acrylate is predicted at 5.76/11.00 mL at 1/1. Its matched-loading 2/1 measurement, 304fb0fdb486ae4b7a07, was 16.43/32.81 mL. This tests the strong-eluent side of a possible sharp response and teaches how an aliphatic tertiary amine differs from pyridyl and secondary-amine examples.

Unseen para-aminoacetophenone at 2/1 is predicted at 9.42/27.37 mL. Para-amino ethyl benzoate was substantially underestimated in c70b471334f9747d6f98. This label tests transfer across amino–carbonyl scaffolds; the different eluent ratio and recorded loading conditions prevent treating it as a pure ketone-versus-ester comparison.

Add meta-amino ethyl benzoate at 5/1, predicted 23.37/42.29 mL. Measured para and ortho 5/1 examples c70b471334f9747d6f98 and 1cee9fb4b0731101f3a6 differ markedly, while 4cb169fead3b3de5dada anchors the meta isomer at 1/1. This fills the positional comparison while retaining loading differences as possible contributors.

Dibenzylamine at 5/1 is predicted at 18.96/34.04 mL. Measurements 6defbf00ecb558b77d50 and 70cba7a21b5a01fb8e73 established a real 2/1-to-10/1 rise but a lower scale than previously predicted. This intermediate point tests response curvature; its 50 uL sample differs from the measured pair's 100 uL.

Measure 1-phenylcyclohexanol at 5/1 and 100 mg, predicted 11.58/15.60 mL. The 50 mg result in 5885d427a26f03e522f3 was 11.17/14.26 mL. This supplies a loading bridge and a matched-loading reference for the selected 10/1 experiment, helping distinguish amount effects from the scaffold's narrow elution interval.

Measure 1-phenylcyclohexanol at 10/1 and 100 mg, predicted 24.70/28.33 mL, paired with the selected 5/1 row at identical loading. Measurements 5885d427a26f03e522f3 and 9ed7c1fb1c2cc499bbf9 showed much narrower intervals than previously predicted. The pair tests whether the retrained response preserves that distinction between onset and completion.

Unseen para-methylbenzyl alcohol at 5/1 is predicted at 10.51/20.87 mL. Compare with para-methoxybenzyl alcohol e4fd83fb3852eb354a66 and naphthylmethanol 614873124b33029a924c. Together with the selected 10/1 row, this tests substituent-dependent response beyond a shared primary benzylic hydroxyl group.

Complete the fixed-loading 5/1-to-10/1 pair for para-methylbenzyl alcohol. The current prediction rises to 28.25/59.58 mL. Measured alcohols show that response scale and interval width vary by environment, so this pair can test whether the predicted steep increase transfers to this previously unmeasured scaffold.

Unseen meta-bromobenzyl alcohol at 10/1 is predicted at 22.18/47.31 mL. It tests transfer from the newly measured methoxybenzyl alcohol e4fd83fb3852eb354a66 and the naphthylmethanol series, including b7cf293311f83700cd9a. Its different aromatic substitution helps distinguish local structural effects from a generic primary-alcohol response.

Measure unseen para-nitrophenethyl alcohol at 1/1, predicted 7.91/16.65 mL, as the strong-eluent member of a fixed-loading pair. Methoxyphenethyl alcohol 776ee2c1e85ebde75168 was substantially underestimated at 5/1. This explores whether a nitro substituent changes the response of an exposed remote hydroxyl group.

Complete the para-nitrophenethyl alcohol pair at 2/1 with identical sample amount, loading solvent and loading-solvent volume. The prediction is 15.05/38.80 mL. Two labels can distinguish an early transition from broadly delayed elution and connect alcohol and nitroaromatic learning without assuming additive functional-group effects.

Methoxyethyl acetoacetate at 1/1 is predicted at 9.85/24.33 mL. Its matched-loading 5/1 measurement d1172a49fca1e196a59f was 35.16/96.51 mL, with a historical V2 error of -67.47 mL. This anchors the other side of that large response and tests whether completion changes more strongly than onset.

Measure unseen methoxyethyl acrylate at 1/1 and 100 uL, predicted 9.24/19.74 mL. This is the strong-eluent member of a matched pair and connects the extra-ether effect in d1172a49fca1e196a59f to the acrylate family represented by 304fb0fdb486ae4b7a07 and 8ebb30a21329a4f7d769.

Complete the methoxyethyl acrylate pair at 5/1 under identical loading, predicted 26.00/69.10 mL. The two labels test whether the large response learned after the methoxyethyl acetoacetate failure transfers to an ether-containing monoester or instead depends strongly on the beta-ketoester arrangement.

The recorded P/O structure at 2/1 is predicted at 7.00/21.82 mL. Its matched-loading 10/1 measurement 902937db42f82f467718 was 35.08/70.35 mL after a large historical underestimate. A second solvent condition tests the response learned from that isolated anchor. The supplied representation does not establish solution speciation.

Diphenyl sulfoxide at 10/1 is predicted at 28.76/47.13 mL, whereas its measured coverage is confined to 0/1 and 1/1, including b2bf97a1dcb9d6609f7d. This tests weak-eluent transfer for a strong acceptor in another atom environment, informed by the P/O failure in 902937db42f82f467718. Loading amounts differ from the measured anchors.

Para-nitrobenzaldehyde at 5/1 is predicted at 8.20/24.30 mL. Its matched-loading 20/1 measurement c28747d70e7b51a1cc95 gave 36.89/82.08 mL. This locates the strong-eluent side of the transition and forms a parallel response experiment with nitroacetophenone.

Para-nitroacetophenone at 5/1 is predicted at 6.66/19.46 mL, compared with its matched-loading 20/1 measurement of 45.32/95.57 mL in b6f1b33a5491968c645e. Alongside the nitrobenzaldehyde selection, this tests whether aldehyde-to-ketone substitution changes response shape rather than only its weak-eluent endpoint.

Nitrobenzophenone at 50/1 and the same loading as ce14dd2481560a984aea is predicted at 34.39/87.98 mL. The measured 10/1 result was only 5.20/20.70 mL. This directly tests whether the large transition is shifted to weaker eluent or whether the model still overtransfers the compact nitrocarbonyl response.

Unseen bromonitrobenzene at 20/1 is predicted at 34.27/68.11 mL. Removing the carbonyl while retaining a nitro group tests how much of the response transfers from c28747d70e7b51a1cc95, 163874b97308a1ea2507 and b6f1b33a5491968c645e. Different loading conditions preclude assigning any difference solely to carbonyl removal.

Meta-dibenzoylbenzene at 10/1 is predicted at 13.21/36.35 mL. Its matched-loading 20/1 measurement 855456da9ea892f7216b was 18.76/48.89 mL and was previously underestimated. This measures the response of separated carbonyls and helps prevent transfer from early-eluting beta-diketones.

Terephthaldehyde at 5/1 is predicted at 11.62/33.64 mL. Its matched-loading 10/1 measurement bae9d67e095423d8edd2 was 27.27/61.62 mL. This tests the onset of strong retention for two exposed aldehydes and provides a second topology-dependent response alongside the separated diketone experiment.

Repeat ethyl benzoylacetate's recorded 5/1, 150 uL tuple, predicted 5.29/16.04 mL. Its V2 was 9.23 mL in a9500e468002e41eceeb, whereas 50 and 100 uL measurements 904c7849feb1c686924a and fefecd79dc057980f62c both finished near 18.7 mL. This tests repeatability of the anomalous tuple before interpreting it as a loading relationship.

Measure the unseen remote-ether, trifluoromethyl-substituted aryl ketone at 1/1, predicted 6.19/13.31 mL. Pair with its selected 5/1 row at identical loading. The extra-ether failure in d1172a49fca1e196a59f motivates testing transfer to a substantially different carbonyl arrangement with low observed similarity, 0.390.

Complete the remote-ether aryl ketone pair at 5/1, predicted 14.60/34.22 mL. Comparison with its selected 1/1 condition tests a new response curve, while d1172a49fca1e196a59f and the methoxyethyl acrylate pair distinguish whether enhanced retention transfers across ether–carbonyl arrangements or remains scaffold-specific.

Unseen dihydrobenzofuran carbaldehyde at 5/1 is predicted at 14.27/30.98 mL and has observed similarity only 0.370. It tests an ether oxygen constrained within a fused ring, connecting to methoxybenzaldehyde 319e89d7000731f64e7f and the new ether–carbonyl experiments without assuming equal responses for equal acceptor counts.

The unseen cyclopropyl ketone with an ortho-fluorobenzyl substituent is predicted at 7.55/15.67 mL at 20/1 and has similarity only 0.316. Its carbonyl is separated from the aromatic ring, unlike many measured aryl ketones. This tests structural transfer in a large catalog family using references such as 3c358af26c2e2988cd46.

Measure unseen para-diiodobenzene at 1/1, predicted 4.04/11.94 mL, as one member of a fixed-loading solvent pair. Its predicted onset falls substantially in weaker eluent. A direct pair can distinguish a genuine response under the recorded conditions from a questionable extrapolation in the low-retention region.

Complete the para-diiodobenzene pair at 50/1, holding sample amount and 900 uL DCM loading fixed. The prediction is 1.25/8.32 mL versus 4.04/11.94 mL at 1/1. This tests a reversed solvent response in an unmeasured molecule and adds information outside the strongly retained failure families.

Unseen ethyl bromoisobutyrate at 50/1 is predicted at 8.11/13.18 mL. The methyl counterpart measured in 933bc87d8ae9186a7803 gave 11.18/19.11 mL under the same ratio, sample volume and loading solvent. This tests ester substitution and branching transfer, with the density-derived amount difference explicitly retained.

2-Phenylpyridine at 5/1 is predicted at 23.46/45.32 mL, but its measured records are all at 0/1, including the same-loading 24e5dc14b855baed89fd. This provides a missing solvent-response anchor for an aromatic nitrogen without an adjacent carbonyl and tests transfer from quinoline and the newly measured pyridyl ketone.

hypotheses.content: Nitrogen-containing scaffolds require different solvent-response scales and transition locations. The opposite historical errors for dibenzylamine versus the tertiary amino acrylate, pyridyl ketone and para-amino ester weaken any common retention multiplier based mainly on nitrogen presence.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: Learning scaffold-specific transitions can improve transfer across amines, pyridines and amino carbonyls while avoiding corrections that help one nitrogen family but harm another.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Do the pyridyl ketone and tertiary amino acrylate show the predicted strong-eluent transitions, and do aminoacetophenone, meta-amino benzoate and 2-phenylpyridine follow distinct response scales?

hypotheses.content: A broadly shared nitrocarbonyl solvent-response scale may transfer between compact aldehydes and ketones and bulky diaryl ketones. Compact 20/1 measurements support substantial retention, but nitrobenzophenone's early 10/1 result weakens this broad transfer hypothesis; a shifted transition remains possible.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: The model needs labels that distinguish a common response from topology-dependent transitions. Existing cross-scaffold observations differ in ratio and loading, so they do not establish a fully matched comparison.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Does nitrobenzophenone develop strong retention at 50/1, and do matched-loading 5/1-to-20/1 extensions of nitrobenzaldehyde and nitroacetophenone share a response shape? How much transfers to a nitroaromatic without a carbonyl?

hypotheses.content: Hydroxyl environment affects onset and completion separately. The constrained tertiary benzylic alcohol has relatively narrow measured intervals, while methoxyphenethyl alcohol is much later than its methoxybenzyl counterpart at 5/1. Donor count alone does not determine an alcohol response.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: These distinctions can teach transferable structural effects on both targets, especially where a model otherwise predicts a generic widening or a common solvent-response slope for alcohols.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Does a loading bridge preserve the constrained alcohol's narrow interval, and do fixed-loading methylbenzyl and nitrophenethyl alcohol pairs reveal different transition locations?

hypotheses.content: Carbonyl and ether arrangement matters more than a simple count of acceptors. Methoxyethyl acetoacetate and separated aromatic carbonyls showed substantial historical underestimation, whereas the beta-diketone and rigid diester selections eluted earlier than predicted. These observations support topology-dependent transfer but do not identify tautomer populations or a unique interaction mechanism.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: Ketones, aldehydes and esters occupy a large part of the catalog. Response experiments across related acceptor arrangements can improve broad structural generalization and prevent a single high-retention label from imposing an inappropriate family-wide correction.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Does the extra-ether response transfer from a beta-ketoester to an acrylate and a remote-ether ketone, and how do separated diketone and dialdehyde responses develop between measured solvent conditions?

hypotheses.content: Ethyl benzoylacetate's low completion volume at the recorded 150 uL, 5/1 tuple may reflect an amount-dependent change or an isolated variable result. The new 100 uL label matches the 50 uL completion volume and does not support a smooth decreasing loading trend.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: A repeat at the anomalous recorded tuple can help determine how much model capacity should be spent learning an apparent loading effect versus accommodating label variability. Recorded-tuple agreement alone would still not prove a causal loading mechanism.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Does another 150 uL, 5/1 label finish near 9.23 mL or near the approximately 18.7 mL values measured at the smaller sample volumes?

hypotheses.content: Para-diiodobenzene's predicted decrease in both endpoints from 1/1 to 50/1 under identical loading may be an unsupported solvent-response extrapolation. Normal-phase solvent-strength reasoning makes the reversal worth testing, but the large DCM loading volume and lack of measurements for this molecule leave the actual response unresolved.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: The paired labels test a questionable response in a low-retention family, complementing repair of large-volume failures and helping generalization across the full target range.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Under the same recorded loading conditions, does weakening the eluent actually reduce onset and completion volumes as predicted?

feedback_interpretation: The previous outcomes support structure-specific responses and reject using one correction direction across polar compounds. Methoxyethyl acetoacetate d1172a49fca1e196a59f, pyridyl ketone 49201b5817f204116f7f and the P/O structure 902937db42f82f467718 had historical V2 underestimates of 67.47, 60.38 and 52.05 mL, respectively. Conversely, dibenzylamine and 1-phenylcyclohexanol were overestimated; their measured solvent dependence was real, but its scale and, especially for the alcohol, interval width were smaller than predicted. Methoxyphenethyl versus methoxybenzyl alcohol strengthened the hydroxyl-position hypothesis. Compact nitrocarbonyl measurements supported strong weak-eluent retention, but nitrobenzophenone's 5.20/20.70 mL result at 10/1 weakened broad transfer to bulky diaryl ketones. The benzoylacetone–trifluoro contrast was present but smaller than predicted, and the early rigid-diester result further discouraged acceptor-count reasoning. The ethyl benzoylacetate bridge finished at 18.57 mL, close to the 50 uL result rather than the anomalous 150 uL result, so I now prioritize a repeat of that recorded tuple over another assumed smooth loading curve. The naphthaldehyde follow-up did not resolve its inconsistent initial record because the amount changed; I do not treat that discrepancy as a demonstrated loading effect. Historical errors guide these questions but are not presented as current-model residuals.
batch_rationale: The batch concentrates on relationships that remain unidentified after retraining: where strong retention begins, whether onset and completion respond differently, and which structural analogies transfer. The pyridyl ketone, amino acrylate, nitrocarbonyls, separated carbonyls and P/O structure receive new solvent anchors connected to measured failures. Matched solvent pairs for methylbenzyl alcohol, nitrophenethyl alcohol, methoxyethyl acrylate and a remote-ether ketone turn structural exploration into response experiments. The constrained alcohol receives a loading bridge followed by a matched-loading solvent comparison. One ethyl benzoylacetate repeat addresses an ambiguous label pattern without assuming a universal loading law. New aminoacetophenone, bromobenzyl alcohol, fused ether aldehyde, cyclopropyl ketone, bromoester and bromonitrobenzene labels test transfer to nearby but unmeasured structures; the diiodobenzene pair challenges a reversed prediction in the low-retention region. I avoided redundant loading variants and duplicate tuples except for the explicitly motivated repeat. Quantile widths were not treated as calibrated epistemic uncertainty: many V2 q10 values are zero and widths largely track the predicted scale. Pure-EA V1 predictions are uniformly zero despite numerous positive initial observations; because that regime already has many measured anchors, additional labels there have uncertain marginal value. Together, these experiments should better constrain structure–condition interactions across the Row-distribution rather than simply adding compounds with large predicted volumes.
